At 4:17 every morning, the streetlights went out.

No one knew why. The city had replaced the old lamps twice, then installed a new automated system that promised efficiency, safety, and “a brighter tomorrow.” Still, at 4:17, every light along Orchard Street blinked once and disappeared.

The darkness lasted exactly eleven seconds.

Eleven seconds is not long enough to become frightened, unless you are already awake. It is long enough, however, to hear things that daylight edits out: the click of a lock turning somewhere upstairs, a cat landing softly on a roof, the whisper of tires on wet pavement, the building settling into itself like an old animal dreaming.

Mara noticed the blackout on a Tuesday in November. She was walking home from the hospital, where she worked nights in the records department. She had been awake for nineteen hours and was carrying a paper bag containing a bruised apple, two packets of crackers, and a small plastic cup of pudding she had forgotten to eat.

At 4:17, the street vanished.

Mara stopped.

Across the road, a man in a green coat stopped too. He had been waiting for a bus that would not arrive for another six minutes. In the sudden dark, he looked less like a man than a cutout someone had forgotten to color in.

Then the lights returned.

The man in the green coat glanced at Mara. Neither of them spoke.

The next morning, she told her coworker Lina.

“Eleven seconds?” Lina said.

“Exactly.”

“Probably the grid.”

“The whole street?”

“Probably the grid.”

“It happens every day.”

Lina stirred powdered creamer into coffee. “Then it’s probably the schedule.”

That was the end of the conversation, but not the end of Mara’s attention. She began keeping track.

On Wednesday, the lights went out at 4:17.

On Thursday, 4:17.

On Friday, 4:17.

On Saturday, Mara woke before her alarm and stood by the window. The street was empty except for a fox near the dumpsters. At 4:17, the lights went dark. The fox lifted its head, as if listening for instructions. When the lamps came back, it walked away.

By the following week, Mara had become certain that the outage was not a malfunction. It was an appointment.

She began to wonder who had made it.

The city was full of systems no one remembered building. Pipes beneath streets. Tunnels beneath pipes. Wires inside walls. Names inside databases. Somewhere, perhaps, a person with a badge and a laminated instruction manual had written:

4:17 — extinguish all lights.

But why?

One night, she took a different route home. Instead of turning toward Orchard Street, she followed the hospital wall to the river. The city was quiet there. Warehouses stood with their windows boarded, and the water moved blackly beneath the bridge.

At 4:17, the lamps along the river went out too.

Mara stood beneath the bridge and looked up.

For eleven seconds, the sky appeared.

Not much of it—just a narrow strip between buildings—but enough to show stars. She had forgotten there were so many. A pale cluster trembled above the rooftops. One star seemed brighter than the rest, though perhaps it was only closer to the horizon.

When the lamps returned, the sky disappeared.

The next night, she brought a notebook.

She wrote: *The darkness is not empty. It is covered.*

After that, she started collecting things people said during the eleven seconds.

A woman on a bicycle: “Wait.”

A boy in a red hat: “Look.”

An old man near the bakery: “There you are.”

That last one stayed with her.

There you are.

It sounded like recognition. Like someone had been searching.

In December, the first snow fell. It came down in thin, uncertain flakes that melted on the pavement. Mara was on Orchard Street when the familiar minute approached. The man in the green coat was there too, standing beneath a bus shelter. She had not seen him since the first night.

“Do you notice it?” she asked.

He looked at her.

“The lights.”

“I notice a lot of things.”

“They turn off every morning.”

“I know.”

“Why?”

He smiled, but not unkindly. “You’re asking the wrong question.”

The lamps flickered.

Mara felt a small pressure inside her chest, as though the dark had a hand.

“What’s the right one?”

At 4:17, the city disappeared.

The man said, “What do you remember when they do?”

Eleven seconds.

Mara remembered her mother’s kitchen, though her mother had been dead for eight years. She remembered the yellow curtains, the chipped blue bowl, the sound of a knife tapping against a cutting board. She remembered being seven years old and believing the moon followed her home.

She remembered her father singing badly in the shower.

She remembered a summer afternoon at the lake, a dragonfly resting on her wrist.

She remembered, suddenly and with painful clarity, the last thing her mother had said to her: *Don’t make a home out of being afraid.*

The lights came back.

The man in the green coat was gone.

Mara looked around. Snow fell through the yellow glow. The bus shelter was empty. On the bench lay a paper bag, folded neatly at the top.

Inside was a bruised apple, two packets of crackers, and a small plastic cup of pudding.

Mara did not touch it.

For the first time in years, she went home by the long way. She crossed the river, climbed the hill, and stood outside the apartment where her mother had lived. Someone else lived there now. Their curtains were red.

At 4:17, the lamps went out.

Mara stood in the dark and listened.

Behind the walls, pipes knocked. A bird shifted beneath the eaves. Somewhere far away, a train called out once, then fell silent.

The sky opened.

Mara looked up.

There were stars everywhere. Not enough to explain the world, but enough to remind her that explanation was not the same thing as meaning.

When the lights returned, she was still there.

And the next morning, at 4:17, the city went dark again—not because anything had broken, but because, for eleven seconds, it was giving everyone back the sky.
